title: Medical and Dental Tourism: Risks to Know First
description: Thinking of getting implants, veneers or cosmetic surgery abroad? The CDC’s advice on medical tourism, common risks, aftercare problems and questions to ask.
h1: Medical and dental tourism: the risks to know first
intro: Every year, Americans travel abroad for dental work and cosmetic surgery, often to save money. Some have good experiences, but problems can be serious and hard to fix at home.

image.alt: Empty hospital bed in a clean ward

cardText: Thinking of getting implants, veneers or cosmetic surgery abroad? The CDC’s advice on medical tourism, common risks, aftercare problems and questions to ask.

sections.html:
• Infections, including antibiotic-resistant infections.
  • Blood clots, made more likely by flying soon after surgery.
  • Differences in standards for training, equipment and medications.
  • Language barriers and unclear consent.
  • Limited legal recourse if something goes wrong.
  • Difficulty getting follow-up care and revisions at home.

Extensive treatments such as full-mouth crowns or “all-on-4” implants often need several visits and adjustments over months. Ask how follow-up will work, and be aware that some US dentists may be reluctant to adjust work done elsewhere. Compare with US options: see dental implants and veneers.

1. Follow CDC medical tourism guidance and see a travel health provider beforehand.
  2. Check the provider’s qualifications and the facility’s accreditation.
  3. Get all agreements and records in writing, in English.
  4. Plan enough recovery time before flying home.
  5. Arrange follow-up care in the US before you leave.

General information, not medical, legal or insurance advice. This post reflects the position on the date shown. Check the official sources below for the latest rules.

faqs.q: Is dental work in Mexico or Turkey safe?
faqs.a: Quality varies widely. Some clinics meet high standards; others do not. Research thoroughly and plan follow-up care at home.
